# Reporting

Every rule here is a bug that shipped, and all of them were the same bug: a
report that read as better news than it had earned.

The reader's question is never "what did you find". It is "can I trust this".
A report that cannot distinguish *fine* from *not looked at* answers no.

Each rule has an **operational test** — a question with a yes/no answer.

## A thing that was not checked must never read as a thing that passed

The most expensive failure mode, because it is invisible. Nobody investigates
a clean report.

**Test:** for every green mark in the output, could it also mean "we did not
look"? If yes, that case needs its own state and its own words.

A skipped check is printed with the reason it was skipped, not left out.
Leaving it out makes a short report, and a short clean report is exactly what
a broken setup looks like.

## Absent, empty, and unreadable are three states

They produce the same nothing and have three different fixes. Collapsing them
sends most readers to the wrong place.

- *Absent* — it was never created. Create it.
- *Empty* — it exists and holds nothing. Fill it.
- *Unreadable* — it exists and would not open. Fix the access.

**Test:** from the message alone, can the reader tell which of the three they
are in?

A read that failed must never be reported as an empty result. That one
produces the worst outcome available: someone recreates things that already
exist.

## A placeholder is not a value

Anything that fills a structure with defaults — `SET_ME`, `TODO`, `null`, an
empty string, a zero — has created a slot, not an answer.

**Test:** if every field held only its placeholder, would this report say
everything was fine? If yes, it is counting the wrong thing.

## Exit non-zero when nothing was verified

Not being able to check is not the same as checking and finding nothing wrong.
A caller that branches on the exit code cannot tell them apart unless you do.

**Test:** with the network down and every credential missing, does this still
exit zero?

## One cause, one message

A single fault reported under each thing it touched reads as many faults, and
buries the one line that matters.

**Test:** if the reader fixes one thing, how many lines disappear? More than
one means they were one line.

Stop at the first failure in a chain, and say what the rest are waiting on. A
missing binary makes every later stage fail on the binary; printing all of
them is a column of failures that look separate and are one.

## Count what remains, not what you found

Totals taken before the work are wrong after it. A thing just handled is not
outstanding, and its old form is not a loose end.

**Test:** is any number in the summary derived from state captured before the
actions that changed it?

## Name the gap, then act on it

"3 unchecked" is a number nobody acts on. Name them, because those are exactly
the places where a real failure would go unnoticed.

And name what to *do*, not which internal field is unset. A message naming a
field leaves the reader to work out which file, which record, and what shape.
If the tool knows enough to detect the gap, it knows enough to say how to
close it — and usually enough to close it.

**Test:** can the reader act on this line without asking anyone?

## Do not let a weak signal gate a strong one

When two checks answer roughly the same question, gate on the one that would
actually be affected. A proxy that disagrees with the real thing blocks work
that would have succeeded, and reports a fault that is not there.

**Test:** is this check a stand-in for the thing I actually care about? Can I
just try the thing?
